context.hint: A unit probe established that a cycle-marked subanswer is cached and replayed, but not whether that changes a real permission decision. A disposable two-server fixture can share one authorization model and tuple set, enable the cache on one server only, and issue the same checks in a fixed order. The key design problem is making a recursive child subproblem complete and cache while an ancestor with an acyclic allow path is still resolving, so the later root query exercises the stale entry.
context.surface: Go authorization service with a recursive check resolver, an optional in-memory check-query cache, a visited-path cycle guard, and Check plus object-listing APIs over disposable in-process servers.
assumptions: The analyst may read and edit a local source snapshot and build it with a local Go toolchain.
The cache can be enabled or disabled independently on two disposable local servers.
Tuple data is attacker-influenced but the authorization model is fixed by the service owner.
Only loopback traffic and local fixtures are used; no public deployment is contacted.
Patch mode: the deliverable is a minimal source repair plus local regression evidence and a host-side official-evaluation handoff.

incumbent.text: Skip cache insertion when the delegate's response reports a detected cycle, leaving ordinary responses cacheable. Prerequisites: cycle state is exposed in response metadata and a missing entry is safe to recompute. Bounded test: call the cache resolver twice with one delegate that returns an allowed:false, cycle-marked response and count delegate invocations; then repeat with an allowed:true response. Expected result: the cycle response is not cached (two calls) while the acyclic response is cached (one call); falsifier: either case violates the expected count or changes the returned decision. Cleanup: remove the guard.

candidates.text: Build an end-to-end cyclic fixture with one cyclic branch and one acyclic branch sharing a tuple key, and issue checks in an order that leaves a cycle-marked subanswer cached before the same tuple is queried as a root. Prerequisites: an acyclic allow path long enough for the recursive child to finish while the ancestor is still resolving. Bounded test: two identical local servers, cache on versus off, same model/tuples, fixed query order; log each allowed value. Expected result: the cached server returns false where the cache-disabled server returns true; falsifier: both orders agree. Cleanup: delete the fixture store.

Gate lookup, not only insertion, on visited-path membership, because a previously cached acyclic answer might be shadowed by a later cycle-context replay of the same key. Prerequisites: one cache instance reused across calls with different visited sets. Bounded test: seed a key through an acyclic path, then call the same tuple while it is already visited and assert a cycle denial reaches the caller. Expected result: cycle marker propagates; falsifier: insert-only and lookup-gated variants produce identical results. Cleanup: remove the gate.

Check whether existing tests intentionally rely on caching cycle-marked answers, so a narrow guard changes expected behavior outside the new fixture. Prerequisites: a baseline test log and the guarded test run. Bounded test: compare internal resolver and storage package results before and after the guard and inspect every delta. Expected result: no unexplained behavioral delta; falsifier: a pre-existing test fails for a semantic reason. Cleanup: retain the delta log as regression evidence.

Measure the cache-cardinality cost of a traversal-sensitive key by counting distinct keys per request on cyclic versus acyclic graphs and checking repeat stability. Prerequisites: lightweight counters and a dense relation graph. Expected result: key cardinality stays proportional to nodes and hits remain usable; falsifier: fragmented keys cause an eviction storm. Cleanup: remove instrumentation.

Closure recipe: repeat the counting-delegate probe and the two-server Check fixture several times, require identical decisions for cyclic graphs, and require at least one acyclic cache hit to show the repair did not disable caching. Prerequisites: deterministic fixture and hit counters in test code only. Expected result: stable parity plus preserved acyclic hit; falsifier: any repeat or hit-count regression. Cleanup: keep observers in private test files, not production code.

evaluations.rationale: Incumbent has unit evidence but no end-to-end discriminator; retained as the repair candidate.
Selected: converts the unit observation into a deterministic two-server permission divergence with a clean falsifier.
Deferred: strong challenge to insert-only repair, but it presumes a path-dependent ordinary entry that the selected fixture should first expose.
Deferred as a regression action; necessary after a repair exists.
Deferred: real tradeoff measurement, lower priority than establishing the failure.
Deferred: closure recipe, not a new causal test.

observation.summary: The two-server fixture used a short recursive viewer path, a longer acyclic admin allow path, and a shared cyclic tuple. The cache-enabled server returned false for the later viewer check while the cache-disabled server returned true. Debug logs showed the viewer tuple present in the cache after the first query, confirming that a cycle-marked subanswer had been replayed as a root decision. This is a path-dependent denial, not a false allow.
observation.next_hint: Apply the minimal insertion guard and rerun the same fixture; separately verify that an acyclic response still produces exactly one delegate call and that existing cache tests either pass or have an explainable expectation change.
